title: Cecilia Payne: Stars Are Made of Hydrogen
source_book: Stellar Atmospheres: A Contribution to the Observational Study of High Temperature in the Reversing Layers of Stars
source_chapter: Chapter 13: The Abundances of the Elements in Stellar Atmospheres
source_edition: Harvard College Observatory Monographs, Cambridge, MA
authenticity_note: Directly based on Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin's 1925 Harvard Ph.D. dissertation, hailed by Otto Struve as 'the most brilliant Ph.D. thesis ever written in astronomy'.
summary: In 1925, young astronomer Cecilia Payne applied Saha's thermal ionization theory to stellar spectra, discovering that stars are made overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium—a revelation so radical that senior professors initially forced her to recant before realizing she was completely right.
content:
In the 1920s, the world's leading astronomers believed that the Sun and distant stars had the same elemental composition as the Earth. Iron, silicon, carbon, and oxygen were thought to be the chief constituents of the cosmos.

Enter Cecilia Payne, an extraordinarily gifted young scholar from Cambridge, England, who crossed the Atlantic to pursue astronomy at Harvard. Fascinated by quantum physics and Indian physicist Meghnad Saha's newly formulated thermal ionization equation, Payne realized that astronomers had misread stellar spectral lines.

Previous scientists assumed that because iron absorption lines were dark and thick in the Sun's spectrum, iron must be the dominant element. But Payne understood that spectral line strength depended critically on temperature and ionization states, not just abundance!

Working through grueling mathematics by oil lamp, Payne calculated the true atomic abundances of eighteen chemical elements in stellar atmospheres. Her results shocked the scientific world: while silicon, carbon, and iron existed in tiny fractions, hydrogen and helium were a staggering one million times more abundant than all other elements combined!

The Sun was not a ball of burning terrestrial rock; it was almost entirely an incandescent sphere of hydrogen gas!

When she presented her draft dissertation in 1925, prominent astrophysicist Henry Norris Russell dismissed her conclusion, calling it "clearly impossible" and pressuring her to insert a disclaimer in her thesis. Payne reluctantly wrote that the enormous abundance of hydrogen was "almost certainly not real."

Four years later, Russell derived the exact same result through independent methods and acknowledged that Cecilia Payne had been right all along. Today, Payne's 1925 thesis is celebrated as the foundation of modern astrophysics.
